title: The Wisdom and Madness of Crowds
question: Why do groups sometimes reason better than any individual in them, and sometimes far worse?
summary: Averaging independent guesses can outperform any expert, yet the same aggregation process produces bubbles, panics, and mobs. The difference turns out to hinge on one fragile ingredient: independence.
content:
At a county fair in 1906, statistician Francis Galton watched a crowd guess the weight of an ox in a competition. No individual guess was particularly good. But the average of all 787 guesses came within one pound of the ox's actual weight, closer than any single expert's estimate, including the butchers and farmers present. This is the founding anecdote of what is now called the wisdom of crowds: under the right conditions, aggregating many independent, imperfect judgments produces an estimate better than almost any individual could produce alone.

Why Averaging Works

The mathematics behind this is not mysterious. If each person's guess is the true value plus some random error, and the errors are independent of each other, then averaging cancels the noise while the signal survives. This is the same principle behind polling, ensemble machine learning models, and prediction markets. The crowd is not smarter than its members; it is a filter that removes uncorrelated mistakes while keeping whatever real information each member happens to have.

The Fragile Assumption

Notice the load-bearing word: independent. The entire effect depends on individual errors not being correlated with each other. The moment people start looking at each other's guesses before forming their own, this independence collapses, and something very different happens. Early guesses anchor later ones. A few confident voices shift the group. What looked like many independent measurements becomes, in effect, one measurement repeated many times with growing confidence and no additional information. The average is no longer being corrected by diverse errors; it is being amplified by a shared one.

Same Mechanism, Opposite Outcome

This is the mechanism behind market bubbles, bank runs, and information cascades. In a cascade, it can be individually rational for each person to ignore their own private information and instead copy the people who acted before them, because the fact that many others chose a certain action seems like strong evidence in itself. But if everyone reasons this way, the group's decision may rest on almost no real information at all, just the first mover's initial signal, amplified through a chain of people rationally deferring to the crowd. The wisdom of crowds and the madness of crowds are not two different phenomena; they are the same aggregation process running with and without independence.

Designing For Independence

This reframes a practical question: how do you build institutions that capture the wisdom without triggering the madness? Prediction markets, secret ballots, and blind peer review all work by structurally preventing participants from seeing others' answers before committing to their own. Some deliberation researchers argue that limited, structured information sharing, revealing aggregate results without revealing individual reasoning, can help correct systematic blind spots without collapsing independence entirely. But the balance is delicate: too little communication wastes real expertise sitting in the group; too much communication turns many measurements into one repeated opinion wearing a crowd's clothing.

perspectives.title: Statistics Perspective
perspectives.description: The wisdom of crowds is a direct consequence of the law of large numbers: independent random errors cancel under averaging, while any shared or correlated error does not, and instead gets reinforced.

perspectives.title: Economics Perspective
perspectives.description: Information cascades and herd behavior in markets show that individually rational choices, made in sequence with visibility into others' actions, can produce collectively irrational outcomes like bubbles and crashes.

perspectives.title: Sociology Perspective
perspectives.description: Social proof and conformity pressure explain why independence is so hard to maintain in real groups; humans are wired to weight others' visible choices heavily, even when told explicitly to ignore them.

perspectives.title: Computer Science Perspective
perspectives.description: Ensemble methods in machine learning deliberately engineer independence among models, through different training data or architectures, because correlated errors between ensemble members destroy the benefit of combining them.

perspectives.title: Political Science Perspective
perspectives.description: Deliberative democracy theorists debate whether structured discussion improves collective decisions by surfacing overlooked information, or degrades them by collapsing the independence that makes aggregation work in the first place.

openQuestions: Is there a measurable threshold of shared information beyond which a crowd's independence collapses into a cascade?
Can institutions be designed that capture genuine expertise sharing without triggering herd effects?
Do online platforms, where opinions are highly visible in real time, systematically destroy the independence crowds need to be wise?
Is expert consensus more trustworthy than crowd averages, or does expert consensus suffer from its own correlated-error problem?
Can an individual reliably tell, from the inside, whether their own judgment is still independent or has already been anchored by the crowd?
